title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
statement: A sorted array of distinct integers was rotated at an unknown pivot (e.g. [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]). Return the index of a target value, or −1. Your algorithm must run in O(log n) time.

nearMiss.why: Scanning from both ends is O(n); O(log n) on (mostly) sorted data means binary search.
Building a value → index map takes O(n), which breaks the O(log n) bound.
You are locating an index holding a value, not the smallest parameter that passes a feasibility check.

trigger.answer: must run in O(log n) time
wrong: Return the index of a target value
trigger.why: O(log n) + sorted structure ⇒ binary search. The rotation only changes how you decide which half to keep.

ds.answer: lo / hi / mid indices on the array

invariant.answer: If the target exists, it is inside [lo, hi]; at each mid one half is sorted, and you keep the half whose range can contain the target.
wrong: mid always lands on the rotation pivot.
The left half is always the sorted half.
invariant.why: Comparing nums[lo] with nums[mid] tells you which half is sorted; its endpoints tell you if the target is inside.

wrong: Two pointers can't be used on rotated arrays at all.
Two pointers needs a target sum, not a target value.
Two pointers would need O(n) extra memory.

approach: Binary search. If nums[lo] ≤ nums[mid], the left half is sorted: go left if lo ≤ target < mid value, else right. Otherwise the right half is sorted: go right if mid value < target ≤ nums[hi], else left.

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
statement: Given two sorted arrays of sizes m and n, return the median of the combined values. The overall run time must be O(log (m+n)).

nearMiss.why: Merging with two pointers up to the middle is O(m + n); the bound demands logarithmic time.
Two heaps give a running median of a stream in O(log n) per insert; here both inputs are already sorted, and building heaps is linear at best.
Quickselect on the concatenated array is O(m + n) average and ignores that both arrays are sorted.

trigger.why: Logarithmic time on sorted input ⇒ binary search; here you binary search the cut position in the shorter array.

ds.answer: lo / hi indices for a cut in the shorter array; four boundary values
ds.why: Only the elements either side of the two cuts matter.

invariant.answer: The cuts split the combined values into two halves of equal size (±1); you search for the cut where maxLeftA ≤ minRightB and maxLeftB ≤ minRightA.
wrong: The median is always at index (m + n) / 2 of the shorter array.
Both cuts are always at the middle of their arrays.
The left half contains only elements of the shorter array.
invariant.why: A valid cut means everything on the left is ≤ everything on the right, so the median is at the boundary.

time.why: Binary search over the shorter array's cut positions.

wrong: Two pointers can't handle arrays of different sizes.
Two pointers only work on a single array.
Two pointers would give the mean, not the median.

approach: Binary search i in the shorter array A; j = (m + n + 1) / 2 − i. If A[i−1] > B[j] move left; if B[j−1] > A[i] move right; else the median comes from max(left sides) and min(right sides).

twists.change: Numbers arrive one at a time and you need the median after each.
twists.statement: Numbers arrive one at a time from a stream. After each arrival, return the median of all numbers seen so far.
twists.trigger: After each arrival, return the median
twists.ds: Max-heap low and min-heap high (PriorityQueue with Comparator.reverseOrder() for low)

nearMiss.why: Binary search needs sorted arrays up front; inserting into a sorted list each time is O(n).
One heap gives one end; the median sits between two halves.
Nothing leaves; the set only grows.

twists.why: Running median ⇒ two balanced heaps whose tops straddle the middle.
twists.approach: Add to low, move low's top to high, rebalance so low.size ≥ high.size; median from the tops.

title: Time Based Key-Value Store
statement: Design a store with set(key, value, timestamp) and get(key, timestamp). get returns the value set for key at the largest timestamp less than or equal to the given timestamp, or "" if none. Timestamps for set calls are strictly increasing.

nearMiss.why: A map keyed by key alone keeps only the latest value; you need the value at or before an arbitrary timestamp.
A heap gives the max timestamp, not the largest one ≤ t.
There is no next-greater relationship; queries ask for a floor among already-sorted timestamps.

trigger.answer: largest timestamp less than or equal to
trigger.why: 'Largest ≤ t' is a floor query on sorted keys: binary search per key, or TreeMap.floorEntry.

ds.answer: HashMap<String, TreeMap<Integer, String>> using floorEntry (or a list of pairs + binary search)
ds.why: Per key, timestamps are sorted, so floor lookups are O(log n). Know floorKey/ceilingKey/higherKey/lowerKey.

invariant.answer: Each key's timestamps are kept in increasing order, so the floor of t is found by binary search.
wrong: Each key stores only its most recent value.
All keys share one sorted list of timestamps.
Timestamps are stored in decreasing order to make get O(1).
invariant.why: Strictly increasing set timestamps make appending keep the list sorted for free.

time.answer: set O(1) amortised (O(log n) with TreeMap), get O(log n)
time.why: Append (or tree insert) and a binary search per get.

wrong: A HashMap can't use strings as keys.
HashMap lookups are O(log n), too slow here.
A HashMap would need timestamps sorted in decreasing order.

approach: map key → list of (timestamp, value) appended in order. get: binary search the last timestamp ≤ t (or use TreeMap.floorEntry).

title: Koko Eating Bananas
statement: There are piles of bananas and h hours. Each hour Koko eats up to k bananas from one pile. Return the minimum integer eating speed k that lets her finish all piles within h hours.

nearMiss.why: A greedy pass can CHECK whether a given speed works, but it can't choose the minimum speed on its own.
Eating from the largest pile first doesn't determine the speed; every pile is finished regardless of order.
There are no overlapping subproblems; the answer is one number with a monotonic yes/no check.

trigger.why: 'Minimum value such that a check passes', where faster always still passes ⇒ binary search over the answer.

ds.answer: lo / hi bounds on the speed (1..max pile) and a feasibility loop
wrong: int[] dp of hours per speed
ds.why: The search space is speeds, not array indices.

invariant.answer: Every speed below lo is too slow and hi is fast enough; the gap halves each step.
wrong: lo and hi are always valid pile sizes.
The hours needed increase with speed.
mid is always the average pile size.
invariant.why: hours(k) is non-increasing in k, so feasibility is monotonic.

time.answer: O(n log M), M = largest pile
time.why: log M candidate speeds, each checked in O(n).

wrong: Greedy would need the piles sorted, which is too slow.
Greedy only works when h equals the number of piles.

approach: lo = 1, hi = max(piles). While lo < hi: mid; hours = Σ ceil(p / mid); if hours ≤ h then hi = mid else lo = mid + 1.

title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
statement: Packages with given weights must ship in the given order on a conveyor. Each day you load packages in order without exceeding the ship's capacity. Return the least capacity that ships everything within days days.

nearMiss.why: Greedy loading checks a given capacity, but can't pick the least capacity by itself.
Packages are contiguous per day, but the number of days is fixed and the capacity unknown: you search the capacity, not a window.
Order is fixed, so picking heaviest packages first is not allowed.

trigger.why: Least value such that a greedy check passes, and bigger capacities always pass ⇒ binary search on the answer.

ds.answer: lo = max weight, hi = sum of weights, plus a greedy day counter
ds.why: Bounds come from the data; the check is one pass.

invariant.answer: Capacities below lo can't ship in time; hi can. If mid works, the answer is ≤ mid.
wrong: lo is always the lightest package.
Days needed increase as capacity increases.
mid always equals the average daily load.

time.why: Binary search over the capacity range, O(n) per check.

wrong: Greedy can't keep packages in order.

approach: Binary search capacity in [max, sum]. Check: walk weights, start a new day when the load would exceed capacity; feasible if days used ≤ D.

title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
statement: Given an integer array sorted in non-decreasing order (values may repeat) and a target, return the first and last index of target, or [-1, -1]. Your algorithm must run in O(log n).

nearMiss.why: Scanning in from both ends finds both positions, but it's O(n), which the problem rules out.
A map from value to its index range needs an O(n) pass to build.
The search is over array indices of a sorted array, not over a range of candidate answers checked by a feasibility function.

wrong: return the first and last index
trigger.why: Sorted + O(log n) ⇒ binary search; duplicates ⇒ two boundary searches (lower bound of target, lower bound of target + 1).

ds.answer: int lo / hi indices on the array (a lowerBound helper)
ds.why: Two calls to the same lower-bound search.

invariant.answer: For the first position: everything before lo is < target and everything from hi on is ≥ target; lo == hi is the first index ≥ target.
wrong: lo and hi always point at copies of target.
The range [lo, hi] shrinks by one each step.
invariant.why: A half-open lower-bound search never loses the boundary.

wrong: O(log n + k) for k copies
time.why: Two binary searches. Expanding outward from one hit would be O(k).

wrong: Two pointers need the array unsorted.
Two pointers would only find the last position.

approach: first = lowerBound(target); if first == n or nums[first] != target return [-1, -1]; last = lowerBound(target + 1) − 1.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
statement: A sorted array of distinct integers was rotated at an unknown pivot (for example [3,4,5,1,2]). Return its minimum element in O(log n) time.

nearMiss.why: Walking to the drop point is O(n).
A heap finds the minimum in O(n) to build; the rotation structure gives O(log n).
The answer is an index found by comparing with nums[hi], not a value range tested with a feasibility check.

trigger.why: A rotated sorted array still lets one comparison discard half: compare nums[mid] with nums[hi].

invariant.answer: The minimum always lies in [lo, hi]: if nums[mid] > nums[hi] it is right of mid, otherwise at mid or left of it.
wrong: nums[lo] is always the minimum so far.
nums[mid] < nums[hi] means the minimum is right of mid.
The left half is always sorted.
Two pointers only work on unsorted arrays.
Two pointers need the pivot index given.

approach: lo = 0, hi = n − 1. While lo < hi: mid; if nums[mid] > nums[hi] lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid. Return nums[lo].

title: Search a 2D Matrix
statement: Each row of an m × n matrix is sorted, and the first value of each row is greater than the last value of the row above. Decide whether target is in the matrix in O(log(m · n)) time.

nearMiss.why: No in-place traversal trick is needed; the rows chain into one sorted sequence.
The staircase walk from the top-right corner works but is O(m + n), slower than required.
Rows don't need merging: they are already globally ordered end to end.

trigger.answer: the first value of each row is greater than the last value of the row above
wrong: Each row of an m × n matrix is sorted
Decide whether target is in the matrix
trigger.why: Row-major order is fully sorted ⇒ treat it as one array of length m · n and binary-search.

ds.answer: int lo / hi over 0..m·n − 1, mapping mid → (mid / n, mid % n)

invariant.answer: If target is present, its flat index lies in [lo, hi].
wrong: lo always points at the first column.
mid / n is always the target row.
invariant.why: Standard binary search on the virtual flat array.

time.why: One binary search over m · n cells.

wrong: Matrix traversal can't find a single value.
Matrix problems need the matrix to be square.
In-place matrix tricks would change the sorted order.

approach: lo = 0, hi = m·n − 1; v = matrix[mid / n][mid % n]; compare and halve.

twists.change: Rows and columns are each sorted, but rows no longer chain into one sorted sequence.
twists.statement: Every row of an m × n matrix is sorted left to right and every column top to bottom, but a row's first value may be smaller than the previous row's last. Decide whether target is present.
twists.trigger: a row's first value may be smaller than the previous row's last
twists.ds: Two int indices (r, c) starting at the top-right corner

nearMiss.why: The rows no longer form one sorted array; binary-searching each row works but is O(m log n), worse than the staircase.
Merging rows finds k-th smallest values, not membership.
No in-place transformation is needed.

twists.why: From the top-right, a bigger value means drop the column, a smaller one means drop the row ⇒ staircase walk.
twists.approach: r = 0, c = n − 1; while in bounds: equal ⇒ true; v > target ⇒ c−−; else r++.

title: Split Array Largest Sum
statement: Split an array of non-negative integers into k non-empty contiguous parts so that the largest part sum is as small as possible. Return that minimised largest sum.

nearMiss.why: Greedy packing is the FEASIBILITY check ('can I do it with max sum ≤ x?'); on its own it can't pick x.
Prefix sums speed up part sums, but don't decide where to cut.
The parts are not one window: the whole array is cut into k pieces.

trigger.answer: the largest part sum is as small as possible
trigger.why: Minimise a maximum + a monotonic check (a larger cap never needs more parts) ⇒ binary search on the answer.

ds.answer: long lo = max(nums), hi = sum(nums) plus a greedy partsNeeded(cap) loop
wrong: int[] prefix sums with a TreeMap
ds.why: DP over (index, parts) also works in O(k · n²).

invariant.answer: Every cap below lo needs more than k parts and hi needs at most k; the gap halves each step.
wrong: Each part sum equals the cap exactly.
The number of parts increases with the cap.
lo and hi are always prefix sums.

time.answer: O(n log S), S = total sum
time.why: log S guesses × O(n) greedy check.

wrong: Greedy would need the array sorted.
Greedy gives the largest possible sum instead of the smallest.

approach: lo = max, hi = sum. While lo < hi: mid; if partsNeeded(mid) ≤ k hi = mid else lo = mid + 1. partsNeeded: start a new part whenever adding x would exceed mid.

title: Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets
statement: Flower i blooms on day bloomDay[i]. A bouquet needs k adjacent bloomed flowers, and each flower can be used once. Return the minimum number of days to wait so you can make m bouquets, or -1 if impossible.

nearMiss.why: Counting runs of k adjacent bloomed flowers is the check for ONE day; it can't choose the day.
Picking the earliest-blooming flowers ignores the adjacency requirement.
Greedy left-to-right grouping is the feasibility check, not the answer.

trigger.answer: minimum number of days to wait
wrong: each flower can be used once
trigger.why: Minimum day such that a check passes, and waiting longer never hurts ⇒ binary search over days.

ds.answer: int lo / hi over days and a counting loop
wrong: int[] dp of bouquets per day
ds.why: No extra structure besides the input.

invariant.answer: Days below lo can't produce m bouquets and day hi can; feasibility is monotonic in the day.
wrong: Each bouquet blooms on the same day.
The answer is always the k-th smallest bloom day.
lo and hi are indices into bloomDay.
invariant.why: If m · k > n return -1 up front.

time.answer: O(n log D), D = max bloom day

wrong: A sliding window can't count bouquets.
Sliding windows need the bloom days sorted.
A sliding window gives the maximum day.

approach: If m·k > n return -1. Binary-search day in [min, max]; check: scan, count consecutive flowers with bloomDay ≤ day, every k of them makes a bouquet.
